content.p: The Cannonball Motorcycle Club was a Finnish biker gang that police and courts had repeatedly described as a criminal organisation. Founded in Helsinki in 1991, it grew from a single chapter into a network of branches across the country. In June 2022 the Päijät-Häme District Court declared the club and its affiliate, Squad 32, illegal organisations, which effectively ended their legal activity. Yle described it as the first motorcycle gang in Finland abolished by court order. The same club's president and sergeant-at-arms had earlier faced a murder-plot trial in 2011 in which the Helsinki District Court rejected the charges, and the Supreme Court has not itself convicted the club as a criminal organisation.
content.h2: Founding and the Hells Angels years
content.p: Yle reported in 2013 that Cannonball was the only one of the four largest vest gangs in Finland that had been founded in the country, starting in the early 1990s. A 2015 Yle report said it had operated as a Hells Angels affiliate for its first five years. Gangsters Inc., a website on outlaw biker groups, said the club was a supporter club of Hells Angels MC Finland until the summer of 1996 and then decided to go its own way. Yle's 2013 timeline gives the same break: the club was a Hells Angels supporter club until 1996.

The two accounts agree on the break but differ on how close the ties were. A 2011 Yle report said the club was formed in the 1990s by former Hells Angels members in Finland. Gangsters Inc. described a supporter club arrangement. Neither source describes the split in detail.

Within a year of the break, the club had spread from its Helsinki chapter to Lahti, Turku and Kouvola, according to Gangsters Inc. By 2005 it had three chapters in Helsinki, Turku and Lohja. By 2013 Yle reported, citing the Finnish Criminal Investigation Service (KRP), that the club had ten gangs across Finland, including a Jyväskylä branch.

The club's early court cases came soon after the Great Northern Biker War ended in a ceasefire on 25 September 1997. In July 1997 a member of the Helsinki chapter was sentenced to four and a half years for smuggling 20 kilograms of hashish from Spain to Finland, according to Gangsters Inc.

In October 1998, three members and an associate of the Lahti chapter were convicted of extortion. Two received two years and four months, and two received two years and two months. A year later, the Lahti chapter left the club and formed a new group called Rogues Gallery, which Gangsters Inc. said was organised with a hierarchy like a motorcycle club. Yle's 2013 timeline dates the Rogues Gallery to 2001, so the two sources do not agree on when it was formed.

In spring 1999, three members of the Helsinki chapter received sentences of four years, two years and one and a half years in another extortion case. In December 1999, two members of the Kouvola chapter were convicted of attempting to set fire to a restaurant in Kouvola after they had been refused entry. One received three years and eight months, and the other two years and six months. Gangsters Inc. said the police still regarded the club as a criminal organisation. Yle's 2013 timeline also lists a 2000 event in Lahti, the Lahti pizzeria murders, in which it says Cannonball MC shot two Bandidos members; the timeline gives no court outcome.
content.h2: The 2011 Helsinki shooting and the murder-plot case
content.p: In spring 2011 shots were fired after midnight at or near the club's premises on Viipurinkatu in east Helsinki. Yle reported in May 2011 that police gave no details and knew of no injuries. A stabbing outside the clubhouse before the shooting was part of a dispute between current and former members, according to MTV Uutiset.

MTV reported that prosecutors sought a combined sentence of sixty-five and a half years in prison for current and former members. The club's president and its sergeant-at-arms were charged with plotting the killings of members who had left the club and with ordering them. The Helsinki District Court rejected those charges in October 2011. It said there was no concrete evidence that the shooting was carried out on the president's or sergeant-at-arms' instructions, and neither had been at the scene. The court also said that the club's hierarchy and accusations of soiling the club's colours were not enough by themselves to prove an order to kill.

Other defendants were convicted of manslaughter and attempted murder, among other charges. The longest sentence was three and a half years, unconditional. The court said the shooting could not be treated as a crime committed in the club's name, and that membership alone did not justify harsher sentences. It also said the trial had not shown the club to be a criminal organisation.
content.h2: Organisation and the prosecutors' case for a ban
content.p: In October 2021 prosecutors asked the Päijät-Häme District Court to dissolve the club and Squad 32. Their petition described a three-tier hierarchy of hangaround, prospect and full member, with officer ranks and honorary members. It said the club's vests showed a member's rank, and that its yellow and black colours also signal membership in prisons, where vests are banned. Police had found written rules in meeting places, according to the petition.

Prosecutors said the club had 190 members, with chapters in Helsinki, Turku, Hämeenlinna, Joensuu, Jyväskylä and several smaller towns. They argued that the club was at least partly armed, citing a large number of seized firearms and ammunition, and that many members had been convicted of illegal firearm possession. They also said the club's main activities were drug trafficking, robbery and extortion, and that its aim was largely financial gain.

The club's position was different. Its representatives told the court that it was a motorcycle club whose members were mostly free of criminal records. Yle said the club asked the court to reject the petition. Prosecutors also asked for a temporary ban while the case was heard. Yle reported in May 2022 that the district court had refused that request.
content.h2: The 2022 drug trial and the Anom evidence
content.p: In March 2022 the Päijät-Häme District Court convicted Esko Eklund, whom prosecutors described as the leader of the Cannonball gang, on several drug and firearms counts, including three aggravated drug charges. He received the maximum sentence of 13 years. Prosecutors said he used the online name "the human animal" on the Anom messaging service.

Yle described Anom as a messaging service controlled by the FBI, part of a wider international police operation. Its users believed their messages were fully encrypted, but the information was being stored on FBI servers. Eklund denied all charges and said he had left the club in 2019. He also denied using the nickname and asked the court to exclude the Anom messages as evidence gathered by methods that would not be lawful in Finland. The court rejected that request.

The case had 22 suspects. Twelve were sent to prison, three received suspended sentences, two were fined, and one was found guilty without a sentence being imposed. Three others, besides Eklund, received more than five years each. The court said it raised the penalties because the offences were carried out as part of an organised criminal group. None of the rulings were final when Yle reported them.

On 8 June 2022 the Päijät-Häme District Court ruled that Cannonball, widely regarded as a criminal gang, was an illegal organisation, and banned it from operating. It also banned Squad 32. The court said both groups had chains of command in which members were expected to follow orders from superiors, and that they were organised in a way reminiscent of a military structure. The club's representatives denied any wrongdoing. The ruling was not final when it was issued.

In August 2022 the Eastern Finland Court of Appeal refused to give the club leave for a further hearing. Yle reported that the appeals court found no reason to doubt the district court's assessment of the evidence. In October the club and Squad 32 said they would appeal to the Supreme Court. Yle reported in November 2023 that the ban had become binding in January 2023, when the Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal.

Yle noted that the Supreme Court had earlier overturned a Helsinki Court of Appeal ruling that had treated the club as an organised criminal group, and that the Supreme Court had not itself convicted the club of that offence. Yle also said that some courts had, in other cases, repeatedly accepted that the club fitted the legal definition of an organised criminal group. Those rulings were made in other cases. In February 2015 the Helsinki District Court also convicted three members under the organised-crime provision of taking part in the group's activity as Cannonball members; the club appealed, and Yle reported that the ruling was not final.

Police said in November 2023 that they were investigating 13 former members of the banned club for continuing group activity. Police said these were the first known cases in Finland of a group banned by a court still functioning in practice. Investigators were looking into robberies, extortion, aggravated drug offences and fraud. Police said they had found evidence that three members were involved in robbery and one in aggravated extortion, and that six extortion cases were under investigation.

During searches of private homes in Joensuu in June, police seized about 500 ecstasy tablets. The amphetamine, amounting to tens of grams, came from a car and a farm the group occupied. Two members were suspected of drug offences. Police also found evidence of illegal alcohol sales on the club's premises, which they investigated as an alcohol offence and tax fraud. A North Karelia District Court ordered the seizure of a farm and other property belonging to members, worth more than 10,000 euros. Police said that people from outside the group were also involved.
content.h2: Earlier breakup and the club's reach
content.p: The club also faced internal trouble before the court ban. Iltalehti was the first to report the break-up in July 2017, and ex-members posted pictures of themselves burning their club vests on social media. Yle's sources said the break came from internal disagreements, while the NBI would not comment on the reasons beyond citing "disagreements". The NBI expected former members to form a new group or join existing ones. At the time the NBI counted about 90 active gangs in Finland with roughly 800 members.

Yle described the club as exclusive: outsiders could join only by sponsorship from an existing member. It reported branches in ten regions of Finland and one in Tallinn. Police in 2015 raided its Helsinki headquarters and four private homes, arresting five people. They found drugs whose quantity was ten times the threshold for an aggravated drug offence, with a street value above 28,000 euros, and two unlicensed firearms. Police also suspected that two of those arrested had helped take over a construction company that was winding down, using a front organisation and straw men to shield its assets from creditors. Preliminary findings said the same method had been used to take control of more than 40 companies.
